The suspect allegedly struck the victim twice on the back of the head with a wooden cane before fleeing. The woman was treated for non-life-threatening injuries and discharged. Regional police stated there is currently no evidence linking the attack to national hatred. by Kyiv Post | Aug. 2, 2026, 9:26 am Flip Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Police on patrol in central Warsaw. (Photo by Piotr Nowak/PAP) Content Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Flip Police in the northern Polish city of Gdynia arrested a 76-year-old man on Saturday, Aug. 1, suspected of assaulting a 40-year-old Ukrainian woman with a wooden cane earlier in the week, TVN24 reported. The incident occurred on July 30 on Zelazna Street. According to investigators, the assailant approached the woman from behind, struck her twice on the back of the head with a cane , and fled the scene. JOIN US ON TELEGRAM Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official . The victim was hospitalized with non-life-threatening injuries and discharged after receiving medical treatment. Following an investigation utilizing forensic experts and surveillance footage, criminal division officers detained the Polish citizen on Saturday. He faces charges of causing bodily harm. The Pomeranian Voivodeship police stated that, at this stage of the investigation, there is no evidence indicating the assault was motivated by national hatred or prejudice. Advertisement Rising tensions against Ukrainians in Poland The assault in the Tricity metropolitan area occurred shortly after the neighboring Sopot city council passed a resolution urging the Polish government to combat rising anti-Ukrainian xenophobia . Recent weeks have seen an increase in reported hostility directed at Ukrainian nationals in Poland, including verbal assaults on Ukrainian minors on public transit in Płock and Bielsko-Biała. This rise in localized incidents coincides with a recent diplomatic dispute between Kyiv and Warsaw over historical grievances. Bilateral relations were strained in June after Ukraine granted an armed forces unit the honorary title “Heroes of the UPA,” referencing the Ukrainian Insurgent Army, which Poland holds responsible for the World War II-era massacres of Polish civilians in Volhynia and Eastern Galicia. Other Topics of Interest Polish F-16s Intercept Russian Il-20 Plane Over Baltic Sea Polish F-16 fighter jets intercepted a Russian Il-20 reconnaissance aircraft flying over the Baltic Sea without a flight plan or active transponder. Seeking to mend ties, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky met with Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk in Lublin on July 29, the day before the Gdynia attack, to discuss bilateral defense cooperation and the safety of Ukrainian refugees in Poland. Despite these diplomatic efforts, a recent survey found that 52% of Polish respondents oppose backing Ukraine’s bid for EU membership , while 65% reject the idea of deploying Polish troops to oversee a potential postwar ceasefire. https://www.politico.eu/article/burnhams.text: LONDON — Andy Burnham flew to New York this week with a dream: the U.K. would set itself up on the world stage as a leading light in AI safety. He didn’t bank on Donald Trump immediately tearing that idea to shreds. The new U.K. prime minister said the country would use its upcoming G20 presidency to set international principles on AI , and use its world-renowned AI Security Institute to test the latest AI models and cement its role as a global AI power player. Advertisement Advertisement Within the space of a week, however, Trump trashed any hopes that America will participate in global agreements on AI and POLITICO revealed that AISI’s usually privileged access to new AI models is now being delayed by the White House – which told leading AI firms OpenAI and Anthropic not to share their models with the U.K. until U.S. testers have finished ascertaining that they don’t pose a threat to American systems. So if Burnham wants to stick to his plan of making U.K. the center for brokering international AI harmony he has to figure out how to bring the U.S. onside, or else press on without the U.K.’s closest ally. When approached by POLITICO, a U.K. government spokesperson said: “The U.K. is a world leader in AI security, and the AI Security Institute continues to work closely with the U.S. government, international partners and leading AI companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic.” Special relationship problems The U.K. already has a track record for convening global meetings on AI safety, but it has also tended to stick by the U.S. when deciding whether to sit out specific international agreements. In 2023 the U.K. hosted the Bletchley Park Summit on AI safety, which produced an agreement on the opportunities and risks of AI signed by 28 countries, crucially including the U.S. and China. However, at the Paris iteration of the summit in 2025 the U.K. declined to sign a new declaration on the ethical development of AI alongside the U.S. Advertisement Advertisement This week at the U.N. General Assembly, Finland and Norway brought a declaration on frontier AI safety to ensure human oversight and suggested a global supervisory regime. It was adopted by 22 countries on the sidelines of the UNGA, but not the U.S. or U.K. Bringing the U.S. to the table on any international agreement will now prove a delicate dance. According to a person familiar with U.K. government thinking, granted anonymity to disclose private discussions, the Burnham administration does want to drive international cooperation but is worried that signing up to formal pacts at this point could alienate the White House. The risks of sticking by Trump Mounting political frustration with the U.K. on AI means there are also concerns that the likes of France, Canada and EU “will cut us out [of brokering] if they can,” said Wendy Hall, computer scientist and a U.K. representative in U.N. efforts on AI. One of the countries that did sign the 22-country pact earlier this week was Australia, whose prime minister Anthony Albanese used an address at the U.N. to reveal his country’s Medicare site had been hacked by OpenAI agents and health records stolen. “That's not a ‘rogue agent,’” said Gina Neff, executive director of the Minderoo Centre for Technology and Democracy at the University of Cambridge, “It's literally a cybercrime against a state. Now, if the U.S. won't rein in these companies, other countries will be faced with no choice: they have to defend the realm.” Testing times Both Burnham and his foreign secretary Ed Miliband stressed at UNGA that the U.K.’s AISI gives the country an edge on AI safety, but the reports that AISI’s access to models is being delayed by America cast doubt over that claim. Advertisement Advertisement AI companies hand their models over to AISI voluntarily, on the basis that it has a deep bench of expertise. But AISI continuing on a voluntary basis is “going to be difficult to sell to domestic audiences if frontier AI companies are no longer playing ball,” said Neff. Hall said that she “can’t see a U.K.-led effort being very strong at the moment but we need to be part of the conversation. Our strong card is AISI. If that is weakened, then our efforts to lead on AI assurance and safety are weakened.” The U.K. government spokesperson said: “We will continue to work closely with the U.S. and other partners on the testing of advanced AI, while building our own rigorous scientific understanding of these systems and ensuring our approach is grounded in the evidence.” The China question China has shown a lot more appetite for global agreements around AI than America, and when President Xi Jinping met with Trump on Thursday the technology was high on the agenda. “Burnham’s call for collaboration on AI standards provides Xi with an opportunity to demonstrate the gulf between the present U.S. administration,” said Aled Lloyd Owen, chief of staff at Responsible Ai, a non-profit for international responsible AI research. “China is seizing the initiative by advocating for relatively uncontroversial measures and a cooperative approach that will be increasingly challenging for other advocates of cooperation to ignore,” he added. Advertisement Advertisement That means if the U.S. refuses to be brought to the table on AI, the U.K. could turn increasingly to China as the next largest global power. The U.K and China already have ties on AI, said Isabella Wilkinson, Senior Research Fellow for the Digital Society Initiative at Chatham House. “The U.K. and China have had very close exchanges on issues of technology, policy, and cybersecurity in the past,” Wilkinson told a briefing ahead of Xi and Trump's meeting. Bridging the divide between China and the U.S. could be a way for the U.K. to bring America into the fold, Neff said. “Burnham has some great diplomatic tools in the toolkit to be able to offer the Americans a way of third-party evaluation for safety, while coordinating with allied countries to ensure that their own systems are safe and secure,” she said. For Burnham to achieve his goal of the U.K. being treated as the world’s “honest broker” on AI, he’ll have to decide how much pressure he wants to exert on its largest, and at present most unpredictable, ally. “As the prime minister said, we are going to put AI at the heart of our G20 presidency and will work towards agreeing a single set of global principles and standards to ensure the transparency and access we need to increase our preparedness – and to ensure that AI development is safe,” the U.K. government spokesperson said. Emilio Casalicchio contributed reporting. Advertisement Advertisement

https://www.starobserver.com.au/news/hea.text: Heartstopper star Kit Connor is swapping teenage romance for medieval monks and the undead in upcoming queer zombie horror Rapture. Connor is set to star alongside Spanish Élite heartthrob Manu Ríos and Midsommar and Guardians of the Galaxy star Will Poulter in the new film from award winning queer Canadian writer and director Jordan Tannahill. Set in Yorkshire in 1348, Rapture takes place at the fictional Lansley Abbey, where ten monks live an isolated life of strict routine and religious devotion. Their peaceful existence is shattered by the arrival of a messenger carrying news of a mysterious plague spreading across England before he begins showing symptoms himself. However, this is no ordinary Black Death. The illness transforms its victims into undead creatures known as “revenants”, leaving the monks trapped between infected attackers and desperate outsiders begging to be allowed inside. As the monastery comes under threat, the brothers become divided between those who believe they have a duty to help the sick and those determined to seal themselves away and protect the centuries of knowledge stored inside. Kit Connor's Rapture is ‘queer body horror’ While the zombie apocalypse is terrifying enough, Tannahill has revealed there is also a gay love story beating at the heart of Rapture. “It’s queer body horror,” he told Them of the project. Tannahill revealed the story centres on a “deep, passionate relationship between these two young monks who have grown up together”. Exactly who will portray the lovers remains under wraps, with character details for Connor, Ríos and Poulter yet to be officially revealed. “I feel like it’s going to be a juicy film — and hopefully, a pretty terrifying one, too,” Tannahill said. The film is another major queer project for Connor, who became a global star playing bisexual teenager Nick Nelson opposite Joe Locke's Charlie Spring in Netflix phenomenon Heartstopper. It has since been reported that he will also be joining the Marvel universe in the future as the new Cyclops. Ríos is also familiar to LGBTQIA+ audiences through his role as queer character Patrick Blanco in Netflix's Élite and appearance in Pedro Almodóvar's queer western Strange Way of Life. Rapture was first announced in 2025, with recent production listings reportedly pointing to filming beginning in October in Hungary. However, Poulter told The Guardian in August the project was then “on pause”, adding: “I really hope I can work with Jordan in the future; he’s so talented.” No official release date has been announced.

Turkey: Steel plant explosion kills 17 in Izmir province Copy/paste the link below: Copy Copy/paste the article video embed link below: Copy Updated: 9 November 2026 - 23:02 GMT+1 A devastating explosion at the Habaş iron and steelworks in Aliağa, in western Turkey has killed 17 people. Witnesses described an earthquake-like blast, while footage shows flames, thick smoke and distressed relatives outside the factory. … More The blast occurred at 11:46am local time on Monday 9 November, triggering a fire and sending thick smoke above the industrial complex. Aerial footage showed emergency vehicles surrounding the site as ambulances transported casualties to nearby hospitals. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT İzmir governor Süleyman Elban said an overhead crane had collapsed into an electric arc furnace during maintenance work, damaging a gas line and causing the explosion. One worker told AFP that a snapped crane cable had sent around 120 tonnes of molten steel crashing onto the furnace, triggering a violent reaction. Around 200 employees were in the affected area at the time, fewer than usual because production had been suspended for maintenance. Five people have been detained and four prosecutors assigned to investigate the circumstances of the disaster, while rescue teams continue searching the wreckage.
